docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
My name is Rebecca Baker, and I am studying Robotics and Autonomous Systems at Arizona State University.

This website documents my individual work for RAS 304, including my assigned hardware, component research, block diagram, electrical schematic development, bill of materials, and power budget.

docs.title: Project Overview
docs.text:
Our team, Team 102, is designing one functional robotic leg for a six-legged spider robot.

The leg uses multiple actuators and sensors to control joint movement and provide feedback. The overall design uses four PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano development boards, with each board responsible for a different part of the system.

My assigned subsystem is Driver Nano 2.

docs.title: My Responsibilities
docs.text:
Driver Nano 2 is responsible for controlling one of the leg's linear actuators and monitoring its assigned sensors.

Component or Function My Responsibility PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano Main controller for my subsystem Linear Actuator A Control extension, retraction, and stopping Motor Driver Interface between the PIC and actuator Pressure Sensor Read pressure or contact information Limit Switches Monitor the actuator's permitted travel UART Communication Receive commands and return feedback Electrical Schematic Document subsystem connections Power Budget Determine electrical requirements

The main controller, managed by Preston, handles kinematics and overall system coordination. My board receives movement commands from that controller and manages its assigned hardware.

docs.title: How My Subsystem Works
docs.text:
The proposed operation is:

  1. The main Nano calculates the requested joint movement.
  2. My Nano receives the movement command through UART.
  3. My software checks the command and relevant limit switches.
  4. The PIC sends control signals to the actuator driver.
  5. The driver controls the actuator using the required motor power.
  6. My Nano reads pressure and limit-switch information.
  7. My Nano sends feedback or fault information to the main controller.

This sequence represents the intended operation. It still needs to be implemented and verified with the selected hardware.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
My assigned subsystem is Driver Nano 2 for Team 102's robotic spider leg.

The purpose of this block diagram is to show how my microcontroller communicates with the main controller and connects to the actuator, pressure sensor, limit switches, and power system.

The design uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano development board.

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:
The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is the controller for my subsystem.

Its planned responsibilities include:

  • Receiving commands through UART
  • Processing actuator movement requests
  • Monitoring limit switches
  • Reading the pressure sensor
  • Controlling the actuator driver
  • Returning status and sensor data

docs.title: Linear Actuator Control
docs.text:
Linear Actuator A is used to move one of the robotic leg joints.

The actuator will require a suitable driver because the PIC cannot directly supply the motor's operating current.

The driver must support the selected actuator's voltage, current, and required direction control.

The final driver and actuator models have not been confirmed.

docs.title: Pressure Sensor
docs.text:
The pressure sensor is intended to provide information about contact or applied force at the leg.

The sensor's output type must be checked before it is connected to the PIC.

If the selected sensor provides an analog voltage, an appropriate ADC input can be used, provided the signal remains within the PIC's permitted input range.

docs.title: Limit Switches
docs.text:
The team plans to use two limit switches per joint.

My controller will monitor the limit switches assigned to my actuator.

The proposed behavior is to stop movement farther into an activated travel limit while allowing safe movement away from the limit when appropriate.

The final wiring and input configuration will depend on the selected switches and safety design.

docs.title: Communication With Main Nano
docs.text:
The team has selected UART for communication between controllers.

The main Nano will send movement commands to Driver Nano 2.

Driver Nano 2 will return relevant sensor readings, limit status, and fault information.

The final message format, pin assignments, baud rate, and communication wiring are still being defined.

docs.title: Power Connections
docs.text:
The design separates the microcontroller's regulated logic supply from the actuator's higher-current power path.

Both systems must use compatible signal references and a properly designed grounding arrangement.

Final voltage and current requirements cannot be determined until the actuator and driver are selected.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page documents the component choices and selection criteria for Driver Nano 2.

My subsystem must control Linear Actuator A, read a pressure sensor, monitor limit switches, and communicate with the main controller.

The final actuator, driver, and pressure sensor models have not been confirmed. The tables below explain the requirements and tradeoffs rather than presenting unverified parts as selected.

docs.title: PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano
docs.text:
Current selection: PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano development board.

The team is using PIC18F57Q43-based development boards for its distributed control architecture.

This board provides the embedded processing and peripherals needed to develop the subsystem.

Requirement Reason Digital inputs Read limit switches Analog input capability Read an analog pressure sensor, if selected UART Communicate with the main Nano Digital outputs Control the actuator driver Development and debugging Program and test the controller

Selection rationale: Using the same microcontroller family as the other team controllers simplifies the overall development approach and keeps the subsystem consistent with the team's architecture.

Reference: Microchip PIC18F57Q43 product information

docs.title: Linear Actuator Selection
docs.text: The actuator must move the assigned robotic leg joint through the required range.

docs.title: Options Considered
docs.text: Option Advantages Limitations DC electric linear actuator Direct extension and retraction Requires suitable motor driver and position strategy Linear actuator with feedback Provides position information May cost more and require additional wiring Lead-screw motor assembly Flexible mechanical design Requires careful mechanical integration

docs.title: Selection Criteria
docs.text:
• Required operating voltage
  • Maximum load or force
  • Stroke length
  • Extension and retraction speed
  • Stall and operating current
  • Mounting dimensions
  • Available position feedback
  • Compatibility with the leg mechanism

Current decision: Electric linear actuation is part of the team's proposed design. The exact actuator model still needs confirmation.

docs.title: Motor Driver Selection
docs.text:
The PIC cannot directly power the actuator motor.

A motor driver is needed between the microcontroller and actuator.

docs.title: Options Considered
docs.text: Option Advantages Limitations H-bridge motor driver Supports electronic direction control Must be rated for motor current and voltage Relay-based reversing circuit Can reverse a suitable DC motor Requires proper protection and is less suitable for frequent switching Integrated actuator controller May simplify control Compatibility depends on the actuator

docs.title: Required Specifications
docs.text:
The selected driver must:

  • Support the actuator supply voltage
  • Handle the actuator's required current, including appropriate startup or stall conditions
  • Accept compatible control signals from the PIC
  • Support safe stopping and direction control
  • Include or support suitable electrical protection

Current decision: The motor driver model has not been selected.

docs.title: Pressure Sensor Selection
docs.text: The pressure sensor is intended to detect contact or applied pressure associated with the leg.

docs.title: Options Considered
docs.text: Option Advantages Limitations Force-sensitive resistor Simple contact and relative force sensing Usually requires calibration and is not ideal for precise force measurement Load cell Suitable for more accurate force measurement Requires signal conditioning Digital force or pressure sensor May simplify data acquisition Interface and mechanical suitability vary

docs.title: Selection Criteria
docs.text:
• Expected force or pressure range
  • Mechanical mounting
  • Output signal type
  • Required accuracy
  • Compatibility with the PIC
  • Power consumption
  • Availability and cost

Current decision: The exact pressure sensor model has not been confirmed.

docs.title: Limit Switch Selection
docs.text:
The subsystem requires switches to detect the actuator's permitted movement limits.

Feature Reason Suitable mechanical actuation Reliable detection at each travel limit Compatible electrical contacts Safe connection to the input circuit Secure mounting Repeatable operation Appropriate environmental rating Reliable operation in the intended conditions

The proposed design uses two limit switches for the assigned joint.

The final switch models and electrical configuration still need to be verified.

docs.title: Power Regulation and Protection
docs.text:
The controller and actuator may require different supply voltages.

The final circuit will need an appropriate power-distribution design based on the selected components.

Items to evaluate include:

  • Regulated logic supply
  • Actuator supply
  • Current protection
  • Motor-noise suppression
  • Grounding and signal reference
  • Connector and wire current ratings

No regulator, fuse, or protection component should be finalized without checking the actual load requirements.

docs.text: Component Status PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano Selected Linear Actuator A Type proposed; model pending Motor Driver Pending selection Pressure Sensor Pending selection Limit Switches Required; models pending UART Interface Selected communication approach Power Regulation Design pending

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Confirm the actuator's required force, stroke, voltage, and current.
  2. Choose a compatible motor driver.
  3. Confirm the pressure sensor output and operating range.
  4. Select and position the limit switches.
  5. Finalize the electrical supply and protection design.
  6. Record manufacturer part numbers, prices, and datasheet links.
  7. Update the bill of materials and schematic.

docs.text:

docs.text:
This page documents the electrical schematic development for my assigned subsystem, Driver Nano 2.

The subsystem uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano to control Linear Actuator A, read the pressure sensor, monitor limit switches, and communicate with the main controller.

The individual schematic has not yet been completed.

docs.title: Schematic Design Objectives
docs.text:
The completed schematic must show:

  • PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano connections
  • UART communication connections
  • Linear actuator motor-driver interface
  • Pressure sensor connections
  • Two limit-switch inputs
  • Logic power and actuator power
  • Ground connections
  • Required electrical protection
  • Component reference designators

docs.title: Microcontroller Connections
docs.text:
The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano will provide the input, output, and communication functions for my subsystem.

Connection Intended Function UART TX Send feedback to the main controller UART RX Receive commands from the main controller Digital outputs Control motor-driver functions Digital inputs Read limit switches Analog or digital sensor input Read pressure sensor Power and ground Supply the controller

Exact pins will be assigned after confirming peripheral configuration and electrical compatibility.

docs.title: Actuator Driver Circuit
docs.text:
The PIC cannot directly supply the operating power required by a typical linear actuator motor.

The schematic will include a suitable motor driver between the PIC and Linear Actuator A.

The final driver connections depend on:

  • Actuator operating voltage
  • Running and startup current
  • Driver control interface
  • Required direction control
  • Stopping behavior
  • Electrical protection

The driver must be selected before its final schematic connections can be completed.

docs.title: Pressure Sensor Circuit
docs.text:
The pressure sensor will provide contact or pressure information to the controller.

If the selected sensor has an analog output, the design must ensure that its output voltage is compatible with the PIC input.

Any required filtering, amplification, or other signal conditioning will be determined from the sensor datasheet.

docs.title: Limit-Switch Circuit
docs.text:
Two limit switches are planned for the assigned joint.

The switches will provide signals indicating the ends of the permitted movement range.

The final design will specify the switch contact configuration, input biasing, and fault behavior.

The software is intended to prevent further movement into an active limit.

docs.title: UART Communication Circuit
docs.text:
UART is the selected communication method between the team controllers.

My schematic must identify the correct transmit, receive, and ground or reference connections.

The final wiring arrangement and electrical interface will be coordinated with the main controller design.

docs.title: Power Distribution
docs.text:
The schematic will separate the low-power controller supply from the actuator's motor-power requirements.

Power regulation, protection, and grounding must be designed using the selected components' specifications.

The final supply voltages and current ratings are not yet confirmed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The purpose of the power budget is to determine how much electrical power my Driver Nano 2 subsystem requires.

My subsystem includes the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, Linear Actuator A, motor driver, pressure sensor, and limit switches.

A power budget is necessary to select suitable power supplies, regulators, protection devices, connectors, and wiring.

The final component specifications have not yet been confirmed, so this page explains the calculation method and identifies the measurements still needed.

docs.title: Power Requirements
docs.text:
Different components may operate at different voltages.

The microcontroller and sensors require a suitable low-voltage supply, while the actuator may require a separate higher-current supply.

The final supply requirements will be determined from the selected component datasheets.

docs.title: Power Calculations
docs.text:
Electrical power is calculated using:

\[ P = VI \]

Where:

  • \(P\) = power in watts
  • \(V\) = voltage in volts
  • \(I\) = current in amperes

For a component with known voltage and current, multiply the two values to calculate its power.

docs.title: Example Calculation
docs.text:
For an illustrative component operating at 5 V and drawing 0.10 A:

\[ P = (5)(0.10) = 0.50\text{ W} \]

This is an example calculation only. It is not a measured value for my subsystem.

docs.title: Total Power
docs.text:
Once the component specifications are confirmed, the total electrical load can be estimated by adding the power consumed by each component:

\[ P_{\text{total}} = P_1 + P_2 + \cdots + P_n \]

The calculation must account for the actual power path so that regulator or driver losses are not counted twice.

docs.title: Actuator Power
docs.text:
The linear actuator is expected to be one of the larger electrical loads in the subsystem.

The following specifications must be confirmed:

  • Rated operating voltage
  • Normal running current
  • Startup current
  • Stall current
  • Expected duty cycle

The power supply and motor driver must be evaluated for the relevant operating and fault conditions, not only the actuator's average power.

docs.title: Regulator Considerations
docs.text:
If the subsystem uses voltage regulation, the regulator must support the required output voltage and current.

Regulator efficiency or dissipation must also be considered.

For a linear regulator:

\[ P_{\text{loss}} = (V_{\text{in}} - V_{\text{out}})I \]

This calculation estimates the regulator's power dissipation when its input and output current are approximately equal.

docs.title: Measurement Plan
docs.text:
After the components are selected and the circuit is assembled, I plan to verify:

  1. Controller supply voltage
  2. Controller current consumption
  3. Sensor current consumption
  4. Actuator current during movement
  5. Actuator current under representative load
  6. Motor-driver operating conditions
  7. Total supply current

Measurements will be compared with the calculated budget.

docs.title: Design Status
docs.text: Task Status Identify power-consuming components Completed Identify calculation method Completed Confirm component voltage ratings Pending Confirm component current ratings Pending Calculate total power Pending Select final power supply Pending Verify measurements Pending

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The power budget provides a method for determining the electrical requirements of Driver Nano 2.

Final calculations cannot be completed until the actuator, motor driver, sensor, and power-distribution components are selected.

The completed budget will be used to verify that the electrical design can support the subsystem safely and reliably.
